item.title: AOC gives major hint about 2028 as Democrat civil war looms
item.description: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she's weighing a 2028 presidential run or a challenge to Chuck Schumer's New York Senate seat after midterm elections.
item.content:encoded:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's political future has remained a topic of discussion within the left wing — and there's increasing speculation that she could be set for a collision course with Democrats' top leader in Congress.

The progressive rock star says she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a 2028 presidential run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker.

"I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a recent fundraising email to supporters.

The 36-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a recent New York Times interview that her decision, which could happen sometime after this year's midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?"

OCASIO-CORTEZ OPENS UP ABOUT 2028

If she decides on a statewide rather than a national run, it could set up a titanic Democratic Party and generational battle between her and the soon-to-be 76-year-old Schumer, who was first elected to Congress nearly half a century ago and has served in the Senate since 1999.

Ocasio-Cortez, in her interview, made clear that her decision about 2028 would not be dictated by someone else.

"I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference," she said.

Meanwhile, a campaign swing the past few days throughout upstate New York by Ocasio-Cortez raised some eyebrows. While the trip was aimed at boosting fellow Democrats on the ballot in this year's elections, it sparked speculation that it was also a move by Ocasio-Cortez to build relationships far from her base in New York City.

Schumer has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for yet another term. When asked about re-election, he's repeatedly said his "first focus is winning in 2026, getting back the Senate in 2026."

Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office regarding his thinking on a potential 2028 re-election run, but didn't receive a response by the time this story was published.

DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

But a potential intra-party clash between Ocasio-Cortez and Schumer may never materialize, according to speculation from plugged-in Democratic strategists familiar with the New York state political landscape, who doubt Schumer will seek re-election even if his party wins back the Senate majority in November's midterms.

"Everyone has an expiration date," said one strategist, who like the others asked to remain anonymous to speak more freely.

And referring to Ocasio-Cortez, the strategist told Fox News Digital, "I think she’s in a good position to win statewide."

Another operative, pointing to Schumer, speculated, "I think Schumer wants to go out on top and with a good legacy and one way to do that is to hand the reins over to this inspiring generational leader. At the same time, New York politics are insane and there are lots of people gunning for that spot and he may feel like he can’t do that."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"He’s always been pretty smart when it came to her," the operative noted. "As other Dems were still warming to her… he was one of the first members of the New York delegation to be very welcoming and thoughtful and worked with her on legislation during COVID."

Schumer's approval ratings among New York voters are deep into negative territory at 36%-54%, according to a Quinnipiac University poll conducted Sept. 17-20. The senator's favorable ratings were also underwater, at 34%-51%.

Meanwhile, 41% of Empire State voters viewed Ocasio-Cortez favorably, with 36% seeing her in an unfavorable light.

"He was the supreme retail politician. Once he became leader, he became a swamp creature from Washington and it started to chip away at his popularity back home," a third Democratic strategist said of Schumer.

MAMDANI SIDESTEPS WHETHER AOC SHOULD CHALLENGE SCHUMER IN 2028

Schumer's short-term goal is to win back the Senate majority in the midterms.

Asked if that prospect would make potentially challenging Schumer more difficult, Ocasio-Cortez told the New York Times, "That would honestly be the best possible problem we could have as a country."

"We’re working hard to have that problem, and I’ll cross that bridge when I get to it," she added.

Recent fundraising text messages sent to supporters appeared to take jabs at the Democratic establishment, of which Schumer is a part. She did not name any particular person in the notes, however.

"The establishment believes that there's only one path to winning: Don't upset the status quo, don't stand up to the concentration of greed taking over our country, and instead spend most of your time fundraising from powerful donors," it read. "But Alexandria's campaign didn't win in 2018 by following the establishment playbook."

Another message said her 2018 victory "represented a threat to the typical D.C. power structure that existed back then and still exists now."

item.title: Walz's 'exit interview' reflecting on his tenure sparks lawmaker debate about his legacy: 'Never serious'
item.description: Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz says fraud shouldn't define his legacy, but Republican lawmakers fire back with a list of grievances beyond the scandal.
item.content:encoded:
Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz reflected on his legacy in a recent interview and his comments sparked immediate pushback both online and from Republican lawmakers in the state who spoke to Fox News Digital.

"Fraud — should have stopped it sooner," Walz told the Minnesota Star-Tribune in a discussion that is being dubbed an "exit interview" with the headline "Walz accepts blame for fraud but says it shouldn’t define his legacy" as he prepares to leave office in January.

"We didn’t stop them. I accept that. I think there does need to be accountability with that. And part of it is that, yep, that’s with me, I’ll step aside."

Walz claimed the state "immediately" took action on the fraud and then went on to suggest the true cost of the fraud, estimated at $9 billion by federal prosecutors, has been overstated and claimed President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, expected to cost taxpayers around $300 million, was more expensive than the Minnesota fraud.

WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT'

"I should have been down on those agencies a little more, but I will tell you this, in the scheme of things, all the fraud that's been prosecuted, by the way, and all the fraud that's probably out there is less than the ballroom at the White House," Walz said. "So it puts it into perspective. It doesn't make it right. Doesn't make it right."

The outgoing governor then explained his hope that people will remember his other accomplishments when talking about his legacy.

"Those are legacy things to address climate. They’re legacy things to address livability," Walz said. "And I get it, that fraud tainted a lot of that. It doesn’t change the fundamentals underneath it. This is the best state in the country to raise a child, and it will continue to be so because of those investments."

Three Republican lawmakers in Minnesota who spoke to Fox News Digital had a different take.

"Governor Walz is correct, he shouldn’t only be remembered for fraud," Minnesota state Sen. Julia Coleman told Fox News Digital. "We should remember him spending our $18 billion surplus, raising taxes $10 billion, creating an unsustainable budget, letting rioters burn down Minneapolis, hurting our students and businesses with lockdowns and pardoning a child rapist."

'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS

Walz has faced fierce criticism for helping approve a full pardon for Tue Lue Vang, a Laotian national convicted of repeatedly raping a girl beginning when she was 10. Critics argued the decision prioritized Vang’s immigration concerns and family ties over the severity of his crimes, with a DHS official calling it "disgusting."

Minnesota Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth is running to replace Walz in November as she heads into a matchup with Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar to be the state’s next top executive. Demuth told Fox News Digital Walz’s legacy won’t be able to overcome the fraud scandal and pointed to Klobuchar’s tight association with him.

"Tim Walz's legacy will always be defined by the out-of-control fraud crisis that occurred on his watch," Demuth said. "Yet Amy Klobuchar praised him as ‘an incredible leader who delivers for the people of Minnesota.’ As the senior member of our state’s congressional delegation, Sen. Klobuchar likewise failed to address the fraud crisis and even skipped hearings on the matter in D.C. Minnesotans deserve better than four more years of Walz-style failure."

Republican State Rep. Kristin Robbins chaired the last legislative session’s Fraud Prevention and State Agency Oversight Policy Committee, and she told Fox News Digital that "no matter how hard he tries to spin it, Tim Walz’s legacy will be that he allowed rampant fraud."

"He says he ‘should have stopped it sooner,’ which is obvious, but he could still be doing more NOW," Robbins said. "He has been silent on fraud for months instead of taking the actions that are STILL under his control."

Robbins said Walz could have taken several steps to combat fraud, including firing senior DHS official Shireen Gandhi to send a message that abuse would not be tolerated, blocking Minnesota from seeking a SNAP waiver that allows applicants to attest to eligibility by phone without recording the call, and asking Attorney General Keith Ellison to prosecute Partners in Nutrition, a nonprofit that administered federally funded meal programs, rather than approve a settlement.

"His legacy will be fraud because he continues to enable fraud, despite two years of hearings, investigative journalists, and Office of the Legislative Auditor (OLA) reports," Robbins said. "He was never serious about stopping it and still isn’t."

Walz's comments not only drew scrutiny from Republican lawmakers but also sparked backlash on social media.

"Walz accepts blame for fraud, but believes his loss of $9 billion in taxpayer dollars 'shouldn't define his legacy,'" the X account for Minnesota House Republicans posted on X. "It does, and Minnesotans are paying attention to his blatant disregard of their hard-earned tax dollars."

Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment.

item.title: Far-left legal 'cartel' in the hot seat as Trump admin decides its law school gatekeeper status
item.description: The Trump Education Department now has 90 days to decide whether to strip the American Bar Association of its decades-long law school accreditation monopoly.
item.content:encoded:
The future of the nation's primary law school accreditor now rests in the hands of the Trump Education Department after a federal panel deadlocked 8-8 on whether to strip the American Bar Association (ABA) of its gatekeeper status following dozens of federal compliance failures.

The deadlock hands the decision to Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent, who has up to 90 days to decide whether to revoke the ABA’s decades-long accreditation monopoly over roughly 200 law schools nationwide. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a Department of Education spokesperson confirmed that staff had already recommended stripping the ABA's gatekeeper status after finding the group out of compliance with "more than 26 recognition criteria."

The advisory body — known formally as the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI) — advises the Education Department on whether higher education accreditors meet federal standards. NACIQI Chairman Jay Greene told Fox News Digital that while the panel split 8-8 on what action to take, committee members across the board shared a core concern over how the ABA is structured.

"The primary issue that troubled all members of NACIQI is that the ABA accrediting body is clearly not separate and independent from the ABA as a whole," Greene said, noting that federal law requires institutional accreditors to operate independently of trade associations. "Everyone on the committee agreed that this was a problem that required changes. The main divide was over whether the ABA was willing and able to take those steps to remedy the problem or not."

WATCH: BRANDON GILL CORNERS LAW SCHOOL GATEKEEPER WITH DEI QUESTION SHE WON'T ANSWER

Responding to panel criticisms of chronic noncompliance, Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA Accreditation Council, defended the organization's historic track record.

"The Council has been continuously recognized by the Department of Education since 1952, being found in compliance during every regular recognition cycle for the past 74 years," Hart said in a statement. "We take accreditation and our recognition as an accreditor very seriously, and we continue to be a reliable authority for accrediting J.D. programs."

However, legal advocacy groups argue the ABA's structural defects and recent policy shifts render it unfit to serve as an industry gatekeeper. Reed Rubinstein, senior vice president of America First Legal and former general counsel at the Department of Education, told Fox News Digital that the ABA has "disqualified itself and undermined public faith and trust in the legal profession."

EXPLOSIVE REPORT EXPOSES ‘DANGEROUS IMBALANCE’ IN LAW SCHOOL PIPELINE SHAPING HOW ELECTION CASES ARE DECIDED

Rubinstein also dismissed the ABA's recent move to repeal its controversial diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) accreditation standard as a "ruse to retain power," arguing it does not cure the underlying legal flaws.

"The DEI accreditation standard, from the moment it was adopted, conflicted with controlling Supreme Court rulings and the plain text of the Civil Rights Act," Rubinstein said, urging the Trump administration to permanently strip the ABA of its federal status. "The ABA's leadership has made it clear, publicly and otherwise, that it will return to its unlawful ideological agenda at its first opportunity."

For more than 70 years, the ABA has operated as the sole federally recognized accreditor for U.S. law schools, granting the organization a near-monopoly over the legal profession. In almost every state, students must graduate from an ABA-accredited law school to be eligible to sit for the bar exam. Furthermore, the federal government uses the ABA's accreditation as the gatekeeper for Title IV federal student aid, meaning law schools must secure the group's stamp of approval for their students to receive federal loans.

BEAUTY SCHOOL MOMS CAUGHT IN ACCREDITATION CROSSFIRE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WEIGHS CONSEQUENTIAL DECISION

If Under Secretary Kent ultimately moves to strip the ABA of its recognition, the decision would effectively break that national monopoly. While law schools affiliated with larger universities could rely on their broader institutional accreditors to maintain access to federal financial aid, roughly a dozen stand-alone law schools would be forced to scramble for alternative accreditation. State supreme courts would also face immediate pressure to rewrite their bar admission rules to allow graduates from non-ABA schools to take the exam.

Some states have already begun taking matters into their own hands to bypass the ABA's grip. Because the legal profession is regulated directly by the judicial branch, state supreme courts hold the ultimate authority to set educational requirements for bar admission.

TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES

In January, Texas became the first state in the nation to eliminate its reliance on the ABA for law school accreditation, with the Texas Supreme Court finalizing a rule to take over the approval process itself. Just nine days later, the Florida Supreme Court followed suit. 

By cutting ties with the organization, the Texas high court announced it would judge law schools on "simple, objective, and ideologically neutral criteria" rather than the ABA's mandates deemed by many as politically-driven.

Other states are now catching on to the rebellion against the ABA. The Ohio Supreme Court formally proposed amendments in May to establish a state-run accreditation process, while supreme courts in Tennessee, Alabama and Washington have all recently taken steps to bypass the organization's monopoly.

"The ABA’s cartel-like control over law school accreditation drives up costs, limits access, and pushes ridiculous ideological mandates over merit," Trump's DOJ said earlier this year. "Ending the Tennessee Supreme Court’s exclusive reliance will expand opportunity AND lower costs."

Rubinstein noted that transferring authority back to the states marks a long-overdue correction for legal education.

"State supreme courts are ultimately responsible for certifying and disciplining attorneys—there is arguably no need for a middleman," Rubinstein told Fox News Digital. "By returning actual authority over legal education directly to the courts themselves... the result should be a better-quality education for attorneys and more accountability and transparency for the public."

item.title: Fox News Media's Spotlight Awards celebrate behind-the-scenes stars as network nears 30 years
item.description: Suzanne Scott and Jay Wallace celebrated the 2025 FOX News Media Spotlight Award winners at an intimate luncheon hosted by anchor Bill Hemmer.
item.content:encoded:
FOX News Media CEO Suzanne Scott and President & Executive Editor Jay Wallace honored the 2025 FOX News Media Spotlight Award winners on Thursday during an intimate luncheon.

The FOX News Media Spotlight Awards are an annual tradition for the organization, and management received hundreds of nominations from staff members passionate about celebrating colleagues who earned special recognition. Winners were announced at a network-wide town hall, and they gathered at Avra in midtown Manhattan just blocks away from FOX News Media’s headquarters to celebrate alongside their families and colleagues.

FOX News anchor Bill Hemmer, who hosted the event, welcomed guests before introducing Scott to the stage.

"In a couple of weeks, Fox News Channel will mark 30 years. When we started, we didn’t have a system for recognizing extraordinary people, and there were many," Scott said.

"We were just figuring out how to not lose a satellite and keep a guest on the air from remote locations, forget about competing with MSNBC, which had just launched a few months prior, and CNN, which was the national leader in cable news at the time," Scott added. "But a lot has changed since then."

FOX NEWS CHANNEL TOPS NBC, ABC AND CBS IN KEY RATINGS MEASURABLE FOR SECOND STRAIGHT SUMMER

Scott noted that nowadays, Fox News Channel dominates cable news and regularly competes with and beats the broadcast networks.

"We’ve also come up with a way to celebrate our most extraordinary performers," Scott said.

The Spotlight Awards launched in 2020, and prizes have since been handed out to staffers on dozens of teams. The annual event gives FOX News Media leaders a chance to show appreciation for individuals who show up every day and keep the company on top.

Wallace then took the stage to hand out the first award, where he was joined by Executive Vice President Scott Wilder and "FOX & Friends" co-hosts Ainsley Earhardt and Lawrence Jones.

The Unsung Hero Award goes to employees who consistently go above and beyond with work that is vital to FOX News Media but often goes unnoticed. This award recognizes those behind-the-scenes stars who keep everything running, often without fanfare, but always with excellence.

Director of broadcast contribution Pat Butler

"I think Pat preceded maybe everybody in this room because he’s been here since 1995, and he’s got some good stories," Wilder said before sharing Butler’s astonishing role in covering the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2001.

"Pat drove the truck down there on 9/11, he communicated with our assignment desk by dialing an 800-number from a phone booth because cell phones didn’t work, he told them where he was parking the truck," Wilder said. "He shot all of those live shots that morning… he’s been an unsung hero for a very long time."

FOX NEWS TOUTED AT ANNUAL UPFRONT PRESENTATION TO ADVERTISERS: ‘WE’RE NOT JUST COMPETING, WE ARE DOMINATING’

FOX Nation producer Tania Joseph

"Tania has been with Fox for seven years, working hard and working her way up. She launched ‘The Sean Hannity Show’ podcast and now handles every single episode. She ensures Fox Nation’s content stays at the highest quality. Her recognition is especially well-deserved, because not only does she have an incredible work ethic, she’s also one of the most likable people you’ll ever meet," Wilder said.

Field Engineering and Scenic Design Specialist Tiger Stanley

"If you’re ever stranded on an island, Tiger is the one you want with you. He’ll have a shelter, a theme park, maybe a bar, and he’ll build it by the end of the day. None of us have any idea how he gets it done… impossible challenges are met all the time. Tiger is there to handle anything," Wilder said.

The Rising Star Award goes to employees who have shown exemplary work ethic and growth during the early stages of their careers.

Assignment editor Matthew Donnell

"We’re starting with two Assignment Desk staffers from Washington, who have done such good work, that both of them have earned gigs with the politics unit. First, Matthew Donnell, who has begun working as a Political Embed, covering campaigns through the midterm elections," Earhardt said.

"Matt always looks for ways to move stories forward, and now he’s going to do it from the field, interviewing candidates, and breaking news in primaries across the country," she added.

Associate producer Jessica Sonkin

"Second, also from the D.C. desk, associate producer Jessica Sonkin. Jessica was already known for her incredible work ethic, and it was an easy call to make her a political embed," Earhardt said.

"Jessica, you and Matt have a lot of long days ahead on the trail, so I hope you’re all caught up on sleep," she continued. "We very much look forward to your dispatches from across the country during this exciting election season."

‘FOX & Friends’ associate producer Carey Gallagher

"I personally know firsthand how hard Carey works, never complains, stays under the radar. She produces segments and handles our research packets. We can always count on her to come up with talking points, good intros and important graphics. Like so many of our Rising Stars, she puts in long hours and is always ready to take on more responsibility. Because of that dedication, Carey has earned the trust of both the ‘FOX & Friends’ hosts and the production team," Earhardt said.

FOX Nation associate producer Sabrina Baker

"Colleagues say Sabrina is exceptionally creative, and reliable. She routinely juggles at least six shows at the same time, and she’s currently leading the production of ‘Park’d’ Season 10. Sabrina adds that she’s excited to keep growing in her role at Fox. We’re excited as well," Earhardt said.

MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME

This award goes to an employee that has dedicated time and energy to his or her local community and is active in company volunteer efforts.

‘FOX and Friends First’ stage manager Matt Rodriguez

"Matt has worked overnights for 13 years. Despite working the graveyard shift, he still has enough energy to volunteer for his Cub Scouts. He’s a Unit Commissioner for them, and that’s a big job. He works with many different packs of Scouts. And he recently completed the Wood Badge course, which is focused on advanced leadership, so that he can continue to help children grow into the best versions of themselves," Jones said.

Washington, D.C., assignment manager Lillian LeCroy

"She volunteers with American Corporate Partners, a nonprofit that connects veterans with mentors for career guidance. It’s an organization Fox has been proud to support and partner with for more than a decade, and we’re so proud of Lillian for her dedication to the community," Jones said.

Lead technical director Rich Cozzi

"Rich Cozzi is someone I’ve worked with for years, obviously working at Fox, we’re leaner, meaner, better and more experimentative than any other network … he exemplifies this," Wallace said.

"I could not be more proud of him… he’s driving automation across all parts of FOX News Media, from Business to Weather," Wallace added. "Rich Cozzi, you earned this."

"Innovation at Fox means finding better, faster, smarter ways to get the job done," Wallace said.

Director Brianne Bombara and recruiter Veronica Baker

The Impact Award goes to those who have had some of the most positive overall effects on FOX News Media. This year, a pair of colleagues from the campus recruitment team shared the award for building a first-class recruiting program.

"People ask me all the time, I’ve worked for 30 years, and it’s no secret I started entry level, ‘How do you continue to have a successful culture and develop great people?’ That’s because we bring in the best and brightest at the university level, and we design a way to offer the best, top-rated jobs before they leave. These two have done an incredible job, I couldn’t be prouder of you," Scott said.

"This year, the team has overseen three intern cycles with nearly 700 participants, made 34 campus visits… they spent 53 days on the road recruiting top talent," Scott continued. "Brianne and Veronica, I’m so proud of this program you have built and, because of your dedication, our internship program is ranked among the best in the country."

item.title: Education Department rescinds Biden Title IX rule, restores Trump-era regulations
item.description: Linda McMahon announced the formal rescission of Biden's 2024 Title IX rule, restoring Trump-era regulations on girls sports and gender identity.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The U.S. Department of Education is formally rescinding the Biden administration's 2024 Title IX rule, Education Secretary Linda McMahon announced in an interview with OutKick.

McMahon said the action reinforces the administration's position that girls' and women's sports should be reserved for females.

"We're just acknowledging that boys and men are in boys and men's sports and girls are in theirs," McMahon told OutKick.

The action restores the 2020 regulatory text in the Code of Federal Regulations. Courts had already invalidated the Biden rule, and the department announced in January 2025 that it would enforce the first Trump administration's regulations.

EDUCATION SECRETARY LINDA MCMAHON RIPS CALIFORNIA TRANS ATHLETE ‘COMPROMISE,’ TELLS NEWSOM TO ‘PICK A SIDE’

OutKick asked McMahon what this step accomplishes, given that her department was already enforcing those rules.

"Well, it just gives clarification to students, teachers, schools, parents," she said. "Everyone now knows what the rule is and how everyone is going to abide by it."

Asked whether schools face new obligations or deadlines, McMahon said they should return to the Trump-era rules. She did not identify a new compliance deadline.

"Title IX was set up to give everyone, including women, equal opportunity to sports. And then under the Biden regulations, many of those rights had been taken away," McMahon said. "And so now this is just returned to Title IX as it was originally intended."

The Biden administration's 2024 rule expanded Title IX's sex-discrimination protections to include gender identity. Its separate proposal addressing eligibility for athletic teams was withdrawn in December 2024.

The Trump administration has pursued its interpretation of Title IX through investigations, funding restrictions and referrals to the Department of Justice.

As OutKick has reported, the departments of Education and Justice announced the Title IX Special Investigations Team on April 4, 2025.

The federal government also filed a lawsuit against Maine over the state's policy allowing trans-identifying males to compete in girls' sports.

Asked about consequences for states including Maine, California and Minnesota, McMahon described the department's use of reimbursement requirements for funding recipients designated as high risk.

THE STATES THAT STILL ALLOW TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS FACE QUESTIONS AFTER SUPREME COURT RULING

"What that means is that they don't get their funding in advance. They have to produce receipts to us," McMahon said. "We therefore can confirm that they are spending the money in ways that it should be spent."

She also cited her department's referral of the Maine case to the Justice Department.

"So there are many kinds of consequences that can come to states and schools that are not abiding by Title IX," she said.

McMahon also addressed what recourse is available to female athletes who have already lost records, titles or opportunities.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

She pointed to the University of Pennsylvania's agreement with the department, which OutKick reported in July 2025. That agreement required Penn to restore records and titles to female athletes and issue apologies following Lia Thomas' participation on the women's swimming team.

"Not only were apologies extended, but the titles were then given to the women who had rightfully won," McMahon told OutKick.

Asked whether the Penn agreement provides a framework for other cases, McMahon said the department would consider each circumstance individually.

For parents whose daughters are told to compete against a male athlete or share a locker room with one, McMahon advised raising the issue with the responsible school officials, including the superintendent, and reporting it to federal authorities. She did not specify how quickly the department could intervene.

On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court upheld laws in Idaho and West Virginia restricting girls' and women's sports to females.

When asked about the legal path to requiring sex-based eligibility in girls' sports nationwide, McMahon pointed to Title IX itself.

"Well, it is Title IX. That is exactly why Title IX was established," she said. "It is in law, it exists, it's a statute, and it should be obeyed."

Let's settle in for another edition of Monday Screencaps after an emotional roller coaster of a weekend that included Michigan fans being served up a dose of karma by the football gods only for me to then suffer through the football gods causing Joe Burrow to fumble.

Speaking of the football gods dialing up an emotional roller coaster, how about the way that game ended in Brazil. The Dallas Cowboys cheerleaders were looking at overtime against the Ravens with the game tied 31-31. And then the 'Boys decided to kick the ball out of the end zone. The touchback automatically puts the ball on the 35.

No time ran off the clock. That gave the Ravens enough time to run deep routes to the field goal zone for Tyler Loop to bang home a 56-yarder for the win.

DALLAS COWBOYS CHEERLEADERS ANNOUNCE THEY'RE 'READY' FOR HISTORIC RIO TRIP, SAPP UPDATE & MR T SIGHTING

All I can think about is Jerry Jones running his mouth about how an old man with money is "dangerous," only for Jerry to hire coaches who don't think through these circumstances. The real tragedy here is that the Cowboys cheerleaders had to make that long flight home last night with an L after they poured their hearts out for the Brazilians. So sad.

• As disgusting as that ending was for Cowboys fans, think about where I'm at emotionally this morning. The Cleveland Browns have a higher probability of making the playoffs (52%) than MY Bengals (50%). Makes me want to puke.

ZAC TAYLOR FACES MAKE-OR-BREAK SEASON AS BENGALS REBUILD DEFENSE AROUND JOE BURROW'S SUPER BOWL WINDOW

• Meanwhile, the Vikings are up to a 78% chance of the playoffs and a 19% chance of playing in the Super Bowl. Kyler Murray, a playoff quarterback? I'll believe it when I see it.

• While I'm on the topic of QBs on teams that make no sense, we have to talk Kirk Cousins and the 3-0 Raiders. Cousins threw three TD passes Sunday and the Raiders now have a 69% probability of making the playoffs.

HOW KIRK COUSINS AND FERNANDO MENDOZA ARE BUILDING 'GREAT' RELATIONSHIP THROUGH RAIDERS WORK, FAITH AND MORE

• The Jim Nantz call of the Tyler Loop field goal is getting all the attention, but wait until you hear the call from the Brazilian broadcast team:

• I've determined that playing golf on Sundays is now great with the NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTubeTV in the cart, but we have to do something about 5 1/2 hour rounds. Courses that see a husband and wife going out need to be paired up with the two guys in their 20s. Sorry, that's the way it goes. We cannot have multiple slow groups clogging up the course.

item.title: Rising NASCAR star jumped, attacked & beaten at America's most famous hot dog shack
item.description: NASCAR driver Corey Heim ate punches near the famous Martinsville hot dog stand after going airborne over Treyten Lapcevich's hood in a wild wreck.
item.content:encoded:
Monday Morning Pit-Stop is a weekly NASCAR column that runs on OutKick.com and Fox News Digital. If you're looking for a normal NASCAR recap, go check out insufferable ESPN ... assuming they still know NASCAR exists.

I tell you what, if NASCAR's big idea to stay relevant during the fall is to just start throwing punches every weekend ...

I think I'm in. It's not the worst idea in the world. Frankly, it just might work.

That's right. Another weekend, another viral fight in the racing world. This one didn't take place during a Cup race, but it did involve a NASCAR driver. Heck, it involved a NASCAR winner!

NASCAR DRIVER SAYS QUIET PART OUT LOUD ABOUT SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM, THE WNBA LOOKS EVEN WORSE & CAR GOES AIRBORNE!

Wait till you see this beatdown poor Corey Heim took at Martinsville Saturday night. Just a brutal attack. And right in front of a hot dog stand, no less!

Disgusting stuff. You'll see.

As for the NASCAR Cup Series ...

Kyle Larson won at Kansas in a race that featured a handful of green flag passes for the lead, which is always a sign of a great race! At least it was a halfway decent finish.

We've also got more fallout from Carson Hocevar giving Ryan Blaney a black eye last weekend at Bristol, but that rivalry is pretty much dead on arrival, folks. Those two spent all week basically dating each other through the media. So much for that storyline.

The good news? Carson's already been wrecked again! I'm not sure this one was intentional, though. You'll see.

Four tires, enough fuel to get us through the final full month of the 2026 season, and maybe a free Martinsville hot dog for poor Corey Heim ... Monday Morning Pit-Stop — the 'Grown Men Acting Like a Bunch Of Weiners' edition — is LIVE!

So, this is the wreck that everyone and their mother is talking about from this past weekend.

Corey Heim — who won Cup races at San Diego and Indy this season — was racing in a late model event in Martinsville. He battled hard over the final few laps as folks tend to do at Martinsville, and got into Treyten Lapcevich after the checkered flag.

And by "got into," I mean ... well, he went up the track, spun Lapcevich, and promptly went airborne over his hood.

Lordy. What a wreck!

You don't see that very often in Martinsville. But, this is also a late model race. These ain't your modern day NASCAR stock cars. They're actually way better, but that's a story for another time.

Anyway, this was a big race. A big event. The ValleyStar Credit Union 300 is often described as the Daytona 500 for these drivers. It's been around for over five decades. It's a big deal.

Emotions were running HOT after this race, especially after Heim parked himself on Lapcevich's hood.

One thing led to another, and, as Corey was trying to cool off with a nice, Martinsville hot dog ... he started eating helmets and fists:

Goodness gracious. What a fight! Well, it wasn't really a fight. Like last weekend's "fight" between Hocevar and Blaney, this "fight" was really just one person(s) beating the hell out of another.

It was pretty lopsided. Corey just ate punch after punch. He had a helmet, and didn't even use it! Again, all of this right in front of the famous Martinsville hot dog shack.

Disgusting.

PS: Ever had a Martinsville hot dog? Amazing. No, they're not regular hot dogs. The first time I saw one, I was floored. They're these tiny, little, bright red hot dogs and buddy, they will change your life. And I'm not even a big hot dog guy.

Anyway, back to Corey ...

"Solid effort, but at least make it count next time," Heim said via his X account on Saturday, with an accompanying picture of him looking completely normal.

Well done, Corey. Solid response.

As for the fight ...

Heim was clearly in the wrong ... on the track. I don't know exactly what he was doing after the checkered flag, but it's tough to pin any of that on Treyten Lapcevich.

That being said, it's a pretty embarrassing look for the Chad Bryant Racing team — including Chad Bryant himself — to just gang up on a kid and start beating the piss out of him when he clearly has no intention of fighting back.

Now, why didn't he fight back, you might ask? I would assume because A) he's got a full-time Cup ride with 23XI lined up for next season, and B) he was wearing a 23XI firesuit.

Would Michael Jordan really care that much if one of his future drivers defended himself? I doubt it. He'd probably prefer it. But, Corey wasn't gonna take that chance.

That's my guess.

Dale Earnhardt Jr ... thoughts on this?

"The thing of it is, those are some damn good hotdogs," Junior tweeted out Saturday night.

Couldn't agree more, brother! It's important to keep things in perspective. Thanks, Dale.

OK, let's put the pedal to the floor and kick this thing into high gear on this final Monday of September. First up? We DID have a NASCAR Cup Series race this weekend, and it was the Kyle Larson show.

Larson led 235 of the 267 laps, scored 76 points on the day, and is now your Chase leader with six races to go.

Yeah, Chase Briscoe briefly took the lead late in the race, but it was never going to hold up. Larson was, by far, the most dominant car yesterday. Barring a freak wreck, he was always going to win — mainly because it's nearly impossible to pass in these cars.

Speaking of wrecks ... let's go ahead and check in on Carson Hocevar!

Eh. I don't know. The announcers try to make it sound like Brad Keselowski did it on purpose, but I don't see that. Yes, Brad is going to wreck Carson this season after what happened a few weeks ago. It's gonna happen. He said as much.

But not like that.

NASCAR'S MOST POPULAR DRIVER HAS A TIKTOK GIRLFRIEND THAT'S CAUSING A STIR, AND HE DOESN'T CARE

Brad Keselowski is a vet. He's not gonna wreck someone intentionally and put others cars in peril. That took out a ton of drivers. It wasn't payback. It was Brad getting Carson loose right in the middle of the pack on a restart. Bad recipe. But not a nefarious one.

Finally ... while we're talking about Carson Hocevar ... it appears last weekend's fight with Ryan Blaney was a one-off, because these two fellas couldn't have been nicer to each other this week.

Frankly, it was a bit much:

Blaney admitting defeat — "I went over there and I got my a– kicked" — and Hocevar in turn talking about how much of a "stand-up guy" Blaney is doesn't exactly scream RIVALRY!

So, yeah, this one is dead, folks.

Blaney went on Denny Hamlin's podcast and talked about eating "two-piece," and Hocevar spent 10 minutes in the media center this weekend talking about how much he respected him.

We can go ahead and put a bow on this one. It was fun while it lasted, though!

OK, that's it for today. Good work, everyone. Let's have a big week and end September with a bang.

Here's Carson's TikTok girlfriend, Tabitha Swatosh, sending the HATERS a postcard from Italy on the way out.

See y'all at Vegas.

item.title: JASON CHAFFETZ: Fox News has never let DC scandals become mere footnotes
item.description: Fox kept Brian Terry's name on the air after Fast and Furious guns walked into criminal hands and other newsrooms dismissed it as a botched sting.
item.content:encoded:
Long after the rest of the media passed on exposing the corruption in D.C., Fox knew when there was a real story.

In December 2009, I sat down with Neil Cavuto. It was one of my earliest national interviews. As a freshman who had been in Congress less than a year, I was sleeping on a $45 cot in my closet in Longworth at the time. Cavuto didn’t book me because I had a famous name. He booked me because a member who refused to load pork into an omnibus was news. Fox was willing to bring on a back-bencher from Utah because the story mattered.

As a junior member of the House Oversight Committee, I did not know then that this would become the only place some of our hearings got traction after the initial press release died down. Viewers who wanted the whole story knew they could find it on Fox.

JASON CHAFFETZ: A DECADE OF SECRET SERVICE FAILURE PROVES THE AGENCY IS STILL IN CRISIS

Start with Fast & Furious. The Obama Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives deliberately let guns walk into the hands of criminals so the agency could "build a bigger case." On Dec. 14, 2010, Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry was shot and killed in Arizona. Two of those walked guns were found at the scene.

The Justice Department’s first instinct was to minimize it. Other newsrooms were happy to call it a botched sting and move on. Fox kept Agent Terry’s name on the air.

We kept asking who authorized a program that ended with an American lawman dead and thousands of firearms unaccounted for. I was not yet chairman. I was a member, but I had been down on that border. Without a network willing to stay on the story, Fast & Furious becomes a footnote and Brian Terry becomes a statistic.

Then the Secret Service. By 2015, I was chairman, and the agency charged with protecting the president had become an agency in crisis: a fence jumper with a knife inside the White House, a prostitution scandal in Cartagena, supervisors crashing a crime scene after a night of drinking.

We looked into all of it. We held the hearings. Called out the problems. The agency’s response was not to fix the protection mission. It was to open my old job application and pass around "information he might find embarrassing." Forty-five employees accessed my file. A senior official wrote that the information needed to "get out. Just to be fair."

This was not a personnel spat. It was a federal agency using private information to punish the committee investigating it. Other outlets covered the fence jumper for a news cycle. Fox stayed on the pattern — and on the retaliation — long enough for an inspector general to put it in writing.

3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT

Let’s not forget the IRS. Lois Lerner’s shop slow-walked conservative groups before an election. When Congress asked for the emails, we were told they were gone — hard drive crash, backup tapes that "didn’t exist." It took an inspector general two weeks to find tapes the agency swore were unrecoverable.

The White House called the scandal phony. The Justice Department declined to prosecute Lerner’s contempt. A lot of newsrooms took the cue. Fox did not. As chairman I told the country the commissioner had failed to comply with a subpoena, failed to tell the truth about what had been destroyed and failed to notify Congress until after the evidence was gone.

You can argue with the politics of that fight. You cannot argue with missing emails and a tax agency picking targets by ideology. That story stays buried if the only cameras left in the room have already declared it over.

I’ve been honored to know and interact with so many great Fox personalities over the last two decades. I got to know Charles Krauthammer in the Fox green room, and on the air when he talked about investigations we were running. We did not always agree. I was in awe of his strength. His was a voice I actually listened to, day after day.

FOX NEWS DIGITAL HITS 165 MILLION UNIQUE VISITORS IN MAY TO CRUSH BROADCAST NETWORKS, NEWS COMPETITORS

One day I said, "Charles, how are you? You’re my favorite person on the planet."

He said, "Good to see you, Jason. You’re my favorite person on the Oversight Committee."

I said, "My universe is bigger than your universe."

He said, "Yeah, well, I’m being generous."

Fox News Channel went on the air Oct. 7, 1996. Thirty years later the scandals have different names. The instinct to look away does not. A chairman can issue a subpoena. He cannot make the country watch. For a lot of the years I spent on that committee, Fox was the network that still would.

Keep putting the hearing on. We will bring the documents.

item.title: Rosie O’Donnell rips Ed Sheeran for ‘siding with billionaire elite,’ accuses him of ‘supporting genocide’
item.description: Rosie O'Donnell accused Ed Sheeran of siding with Robert Kraft and of "supporting genocide" after Macklemore was dropped from the "Loop Tour."
item.content:encoded:
Rosie O'Donnell blasted New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and singer Ed Sheeran on Friday during an appearance on Ireland's "The Late Late Show," accusing Sheeran of making a "very bad mistake" after Macklemore was removed from his U.S. tour following the rapper's pro-Palestinian performances.

O’Donnell made the accusation after host Patrick Kielty asked about the controversy surrounding Kraft, Sheeran and Macklemore.

"I think Ed Sheeran made a very bad mistake and that he will come to understand the ramifications of siding with a billionaire elite, in supporting genocide rather than the people who are saying, 'This is wrong. We will not stand for it. We are human beings and each human life matters and that's what's the most important thing,'" O’Donnell said.

LIBERAL LAWMAKERS, ACTIVISTS RALLY BEHIND MACKLEMORE AFTER SHEERAN TOUR REMOVAL OVER 'FREE PALESTINE' STANCE

"Hollywood in Toto" host Christian Toto said celebrities face pressure within the entertainment industry to adopt a particular position on the Israel-Palestinian conflict and compared the dynamic to the entertainment industry’s response to Black Lives Matter.

"There is only one acceptable answer for celebrities when it comes to the ongoing Israel/Palestinian conflict. Say 'Free Palestine' and nothing else," Toto told Fox News Digital in comments Sunday. "It's the new BLM, a contentious issue where celebrities know they'll gain approval within their circle by repeating that mantra. They also understand they won't be pressured to defend their point of view by the vast majority of entertainment reporters. It's a safe space for them. Journalists now know they can pepper stars with similar questions and get a similar response (and lots of clicks for their interviews)."

"Most artists know better than to alienate audiences with their political views," he continued. "The Springsteens, Morellos and Macklemores remain the exception. Concert ticket prices are too high for most bands to get on their soapbox and risk dooming repeat business. Actors don't make the connection between their divisive words and audience reaction. They simply want to appease their fellow actors and make nice with potential directors and casting directors. So they read from the approved script."

ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL

O'Donnell directly targeted Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium and founded the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, after Kielty referenced Kraft's role in opposing Macklemore's appearance at the venue.

"Well, he's part of the billionaire elite," she said. "Those are the most corrupt people in the United States right now. And they have sort of performed a coup on the American government. And it's very tragic."

Nick Fondacaro, associate editor for NewsBusters, reacted to O'Donnell's comments, saying, "Are we surprised that an unabashed 9/11-truther took an irrational and unhinged position?"

"It’s irresponsible and incendiary to claim a coup has taken place in America, especially when political violence is on the rise. Given that people like Charlie Kirk and Brian Thompson have been killed by leftists for their political causes, Rosie’s prediction that Sheeran will come to learn a lesson sounded like a warning or threat," he continued. "It’s hypocritical that a multimillionaire like Rosie things that Robert Kraft didn’t have the same rights as she and Macklemore. The stadium is his property, and he can decide who to allow in or not, just like they can bar Kraft from their multimillion-dollar mansions."

Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran's "Loop Tour" after repeatedly saying "Free Palestine" and performing "Hind's Hall" during shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The rapper alleged Kraft told Sheeran he would not be permitted to perform at Gillette Stadium and rallied other venue owners against his continued participation. Tour promoter Messina Touring Group said venues had informed them they would not allow concerts to proceed with Macklemore on the lineup.

ROBERT KRAFT, GILLETTE STADIUM BOOT MACKLEMORE FROM ED SHEERAN TOUR OVER ‘FREE PALESTINE’ RANT

Kraft defended his position by citing what he described as Macklemore's "broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery," while stressing that his decision was not intended to dismiss Palestinian suffering. Kraft said support for Palestinians and opposition to Hamas and antisemitism were compatible positions.

"Standing with the Palestinian people and standing against Hamas, antisemitism and hate should not be mutually exclusive," Kraft said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Sheeran has also publicly rejected the implication that he supports the suffering of Palestinians. During his first concert after the controversy, Fox News Digital reported from Philadelphia that Sheeran condemned Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack while also criticizing the scale of civilian suffering in Gaza.

"What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate," Sheeran said.

Sheeran also pledged $2 million toward humanitarian relief and asked Kraft to match the contribution. Kraft agreed, saying he had spent decades supporting programs bringing Palestinians and Israelis together. Macklemore separately pledged the $1 million he said he earned from the tour to Palestinian aid organizations.

Fox News Digital reached out to Kraft, Sheeran and Macklemore for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

item.title: I'm 25 with a terminal disease. We need an FDA commissioner that hears people like me
item.description: A 25-year-old living with Duchenne muscular dystrophy explains why the Senate confirmation fight over FDA nominee Dr. Heidi Overton is personal.
item.content:encoded:
I just turned 25.

People with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) aren't expected to see another birthday after this one. DMD is a progressive disease; my muscles weaken over time and things that used to be automatic now take planning, assistance, or simply aren't possible anymore. Even sleeping can be hard. Bed sores are now an issue. Basic physical function takes work most people never have to think about.

I know what the statistics say. I am not ready to let them write the ending of my story.

TRUMP FDA PICK REPEATEDLY SIDESTEPS SANDERS' UNIVERSAL HEALTHCARE DEMANDS IN HEATED CLASH

I want to grow my career, I want to get married and start a family. I want to wake up decades from now and realize that turning 25 wasn't the beginning of the end — it was just another birthday I was blessed enough to reach.

That's why I'm watching the Senate confirmation fight over Dr. Heidi Overton, the nominee to lead the FDA, more closely than most 25-year-olds ever watch Washington.

For most Americans, an FDA commissioner is just another name in the news. For the 30 million Americans like me living with a rare disease, that person can decide how many options I have and how much time I have to use them.

To be clear: I'm not asking the FDA to abandon science. I respect doctors, clinical trials and hard evidence. I know some drugs don't work and some carry real risk.

But there's a question Washington doesn't ask often enough: who gets to decide how much risk a patient is willing to accept?

If I understand the risks, my doctor understands the risks, and there's real evidence a treatment could help, why does a regulator in Washington get the final word on whether I'm allowed to try?

Congress already recognized part of this principle when President Trump signed the Right to Try Act into law in 2018. That law was a major step forward because it affirmed something patients facing life-threatening diseases have always known: when approved options are exhausted, and a doctor believes an investigational treatment may help, patients should not be treated as passive observers in their own survival.

Right to Try was not the end of that idea. It was the beginning of a patient-centered philosophy that should shape the FDA’s culture more broadly. The same principle should apply when the agency weighs evidence, risk, urgency and access for rare-disease patients. If the patient understands the risk, the physician understands the risk, and there is real evidence that a treatment could help, the system should lean toward partnership instead of paternalism.

That’s why Senator Ron Johnson and Representative Diana Harshbarger introduced Right to Try 2.0: to carry that same principle into the next era of medicine, including individualized treatments that do not fit neatly into the FDA’s traditional approval model. They are right to press the issue. But the next leader at the FDA should not have to wait for Congress to force a more patient-centered approach.

The FDA already knows that time matters. Its accelerated approval pathway exists precisely because making patients with serious, life-threatening diseases wait years for a traditional clinical endpoint can cost them the thing they can't get back. The agency has used that pathway for multiple DMD treatments already.

FIRST-EVER GENE THERAPY FOR HEARING LOSS GETS FDA APPROVAL: 'GROUNDBREAKING'

Because waiting is never neutral when you have Duchenne. Every year can mean another loss of strength, another limitation, another piece of independence gone for good.

My brother, who also lives with DMD, has seen the other side of this fight, too. Even when a treatment exists, actually getting it can be its own battle. Traveling hours away from home for a multiyear clinical trial sounds manageable in a Washington conference room. It looks very different when you're the one making that trip while your body is working against you as opposed to having access to the therapy at your own hospital.

CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

That's why I want the next FDA commissioner to listen to patients like me. We don’t just read about the disease in books or look at it through a microscope — we live with it every day. It’s in us — woven into our DNA. Living with Duchenne has forced me to learn more about drug development and regulatory pathways than I ever expected to know.

I want an FDA that works with patients, physicians and rare-disease experts. That's also why I'm going to say something people will have opinions about: I hope whoever leads the FDA brings on Dr. Houman Hemmati as deputy commissioner. He has spent his career in biotech, not politics, building treatments for rare and degenerative diseases instead of just regulating them from the outside. He's also my friend. I know what that sentence invites. Critics will say I'm just trying to get someone I know into the room. They're right that I know him. What they're missing is: he doesn't just know my disease, he's lived it with me.

I'm not asking anyone to promise me forever. I'm asking for the chance to fight for the future I still see.

I've already outlived what a lot of people expected. I'm not ready to stop.

Senators considering Dr. Overton's nomination have a choice to make too: confirm a commissioner who will treat patients as partners in their own survival, or keep a system that treats us as bystanders to it.

It's time. And I'd like Washington to finally understand what mine is worth.
